query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled plasma-assisted nitriding treatment to form a thin, adherent boron nitride (BN) diffusion-barrier layer on boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten aluminum corrosion by impeding aluminum infiltration and reaction with the substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with conventional boride surface layers as produced by standard boriding treatments.
generation.intervention: Subject the components to a nitrogen-rich plasma treatment at approximately 900 °C for 2–4 hours under low-pressure conditions (~10−2–10−3 mbar) to form a homogeneous ~3–5 µm thick BN layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in molten aluminum environments as encountered during hot-dip aluminum-plating operations.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, uniform BN diffusion-barrier layer on the surface of the boride component.
generation.mechanism: The BN layer, being chemically stable and inert at high temperatures, slows the diffusion of aluminum into the boride substrate, thereby inhibiting corrosive reactions and degradation under prolonged exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: The plasma-assisted nitrided components will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate and improved structural integrity relative to untreated boride-based components when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Standard boride-based components without the BN barrier layer treatment.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected provided that the BN layer maintains its uniform thickness (3–5 µm) and adhesion under thermal cycling; the intervention’s benefits are limited to environments with temperatures around 900 °C as typical in hot-dip aluminum-plating processes.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the long-term stability of the BN layer under repeated thermal cycling and mechanical stresses, which could affect its barrier properties over extended operational periods.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based component samples: one set will undergo the plasma-assisted nitriding treatment to deposit a BN layer, and the other will remain untreated as the baseline. Expose both sets to molten aluminum under controlled laboratory conditions mimicking hot-dip aluminum plating (temperature around 900 °C in a molten aluminum bath for a predetermined duration).
measurements: Quantify the corrosion depth and rate using cross-sectional microscopy (e.g., SEM/EDS) after exposure.
Assess surface integrity and adhesion of the BN layer via microstructural analysis.
Measure any changes in mechanical hardness or residual strength post-exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate or improvement in structural integrity compared to the untreated samples, or if the BN layer degrades or delaminates under the test conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys were treated by powder-pack boriding to improve their surface hardness and wear resistance. The variation of boriding layer thickness with time and temperature was studied. Then, the frequency factor D0 and diffusion activation energy Q of element B in HEA are calculated to be 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s and 206.93 kJ/mol, respectively. The diffusion behavior of elements in the boronizing process was investigated and shows that the boride layer forms with the metal atoms diffusing outward and the diffusion layer forms with the B atoms diffusing inward by the Pt-labeling method. In addition, the surface microhardness of CoCrFeNiMn HEA was significantly improved to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa, and the friction coefficient was reduced from 0.86 to 0.48~0.61.Keywords: high entropy alloy, boronizing, growth kinetics, boronizing mechanism, wear resistance

In this work, a reinforced layer on the surface of HEA was successfully synthesized by powder-pack boriding. The microstructure, microhardness, wear resistance, and boriding mechanism were investigated. The following conclusions can be summarized: The microstructure of the surface layer is mainly composed of MB-type boride and M2B-type boride. The original interface of the surface layer is located at the interface between the BL and the diffusion layer, where element B diffuses inward and metal elements diffuse outward. The activation energy and frequency factor of the B element in CoCrFeMnNi HEA are 206.93 kJ/mol and 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s, respectively. Increasing the boronizing duration and temperature resulted in an increase in the BL and diffusion layer thickness. The surface strengthening of CoCrFeMnNi HEA was achieved by the boriding treatment. Its surface microhardness has significantly increased from 3.9 ± 0.1 Gpa to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa. The surface layer shows a lower friction coefficient of 0.48 than that of the substrate (0.86). Depending on the wear mechanism, adhesive wear mainly occurs in unboronized samples, and abrasive wear is the main wear mechanism in boronized samples. Th

Tests of the synthesized materials in a high-temperature oxidizing gas flow showed that with an increase in the content of Zr and Hf in the composition, the temperature of the formation of the liquid phase on the surface of the sample increases; therefore, the maximum temperature without intensive entrainment and the potential operating time of the material increase. The proposed method for the synthesis of high-entropy ceramics has the following advantages: it makes it possible to obtain materials that are single-phase and homogeneous in chemical composition, the minimum content of impurity phases, a controlled synthesis process, repeatability of results and the possibility of scaling.

decision.trend: Prior research on boronizing boride- or boron-containing alloys (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys) has shown that creating dense boride layers can significantly enhance hardness and wear resistance in harsh environments. However, while boriding has improved performance against oxidation or certain molten salts, its long-term efficacy against molten aluminum corrosion remains less explored. Studies demonstrate that a carefully tailored surface modification—notably forming stable, inert, or slowly growing boride-containing layers—can slow down diffusion-controlled corrosion and wear. Although these techniques showed promise in some high-temperature media, the challenge of sustained exposure to reactive molten aluminum remains insufficiently solved.
decision.unsolved: Despite successes in applying boriding to high-entropy alloys and steel, how best to protect boride-based components in continuous contact with aggressively molten aluminum has not been fully resolved. Key unanswered questions include how to tailor surface modifications for stable, adherent, and chemically inert layers that can resist aluminum infiltration and dissolution over the cyclic thermal conditions of hot-dip aluminum-plating operations.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled plasma-assisted nitriding treatment to form a thin, adherent boron nitride (BN) diffusion-barrier layer on the existing boride substrate. Process parameters include a nitrogen-rich plasma at 900 °C for 2–4 hours at ~10−2–10−3 mbar, ensuring a homogeneous BN layer thickness of 3–5 micrometers.
decision.why: BN is chemically stable in high-temperature, molten-Al environments and can impede aluminum infiltration and reaction with borides. Growing a BN layer builds on the proven success of boron-based diffusion coatings, as in previous boronizing studies (PMC10221107), yet adds further chemical inertness and improved long-term performance in molten aluminum. The proposed nitriding step leverages existing surface engineering practices to create a robust barrier layer with efficacy in high-temperature aluminum plating conditions.
